ladder.w: Reading a value the CPU core used a moment ago. The core keeps a tiny, very fast memory (the L1 cache, tens of kilobytes) right next to it.

pts.note: 0.98 ns per dependent load, 64 KiB working set (fits in the 128 KiB L1).
pts.label: M1 Pro

pts.note: Zen 5 keeps a 4-cycle load-to-use latency (Chips and Cheese, Hot Chips 2024); 4 cycles at 5.0 GHz = 0.8 ns (clock chosen for illustration).
pts.label: Zen 5, 4 cycles

ladder.w: The next, larger cache (megabytes). Still on the chip, a few times slower than L1.

pts.note: 5.63 ns, 512 KiB working set (M1 Pro has a 12 MiB L2 shared by a cluster).
pts.label: M1 Pro

ladder.w: Fetching a value that is in none of the caches, from the RAM sticks. The classic "100 ns" has barely moved in 25 years, while CPUs got much faster: that gap is why caches exist.

pts.note: "just over 70 ns" on a Ryzen 9 9950X with DDR5-6000 (a desktop; servers are typically slower, the same source notes).
pts.label: Ryzen 9950X

pts.note: 126 ns with a 512 MiB working set; includes address-translation (TLB) misses, as real random access does.
pts.label: M1 Pro

ladder.w: Streaming through a megabyte in order. Sequential reads are fast because the hardware prefetches the next bytes before you ask.

pts.note: One thread summing a 1 GiB array: 57.4 GB/s, so 18.3 microseconds per MiB. About 14 times faster than the classic figure.
pts.label: M1 Pro, 1 thread

ladder.n: Write 4 KiB to a file (no fsync)
ladder.w: A normal write only copies your bytes into the operating system's page cache (RAM it uses to hold file data). It returns before anything touches the disk: fast, but lost if the power fails.

pts.note: Median 2.2 microseconds.
pts.label: M1 Pro

ladder.n: SSD random read (NVMe, one at a time)
ladder.w: Reading one small block from a random place on a solid-state drive, waiting for each read before issuing the next ("queue depth 1"). NVMe is the fast interface modern SSDs use.

pts.note: fio average 102 microseconds for 8 KB reads at io_depth 1 (about 11 of them are kernel CPU), consumer Crucial P3, 2025.
pts.label: Crucial P3

ladder.n: fsync, datacenter SSD with power-loss protection
ladder.w: fsync asks the OS to push a file's data all the way to stable storage and wait. A datacenter SSD with power-loss protection (capacitors that finish writes if power fails) can acknowledge as soon as the data is in its own cache.

pts.note: Samsung PM9A3: 1.6 microseconds per fsync after a 16 KB write.
pts.label: PM9A3

pts.note: Intel/Solidigm D7-P5520 (Hetzner server, RAID 1): 12.4 microseconds.
pts.label: D7-P5520

ladder.w: The same durable write on rented cloud storage. A local NVMe disk attached to the VM is fast; a network block disk (the default "persistent disk" kind) adds a network round trip per flush.

pts.note: Google Cloud c3d local NVMe (RAID 0, ext4): 56 microseconds; xfs 40.
pts.label: GCP local NVMe

pts.note: Google Cloud Hyperdisk Balanced (network-attached, ext4): 738 microseconds per fsync; fdatasync only 47.
pts.label: GCP Hyperdisk

ladder.w: Laptop and desktop SSDs usually lack power-loss protection, so a real flush must wait until the data is written to flash.

pts.note: Crucial T500 (consumer NVMe; the author notes claims that it has PLP): 891 microseconds.
pts.label: Crucial T500

pts.note: Samsung 990 Pro (consumer NVMe, no PLP): 2,974 microseconds, about 3 ms.
pts.label: Samsung 990 Pro

pts.note: Samsung 960 Pro (high-end consumer NVMe, 2018): 3.8 ms; Intel P3700 (enterprise, PLP): 0.14 ms.
pts.label: 2018: 960 Pro

ladder.n: fsync on a Mac: the trap
ladder.w: On macOS, plain fsync() returns once the drive has the data in its volatile cache; only fcntl(F_FULLFSYNC) forces a real flush. Databases on macOS must choose which they use (PostgreSQL's fsync_writethrough).

pts.note: fsync(): median 29.7 microseconds (not durable against power loss).
pts.label: fsync()

pts.note: F_FULLFSYNC: median 4.4 ms, p99 10.0 ms: about 147 times slower.
pts.label: F_FULLFSYNC

ladder.w: A spinning disk must move its arm and wait for the platter to rotate under it. At 7,200 rpm half a rotation alone is 4.2 ms.

pts.note: Average rotational wait = half a turn = 60 / 7200 / 2 = 4.17 ms (before any arm movement).
pts.label: half rotation

pts.note: 7,200 rpm desktop SATA drives: 17 to 25 ms per fsync (about two rotations); 5,400 rpm: 45 to 66 ms.
pts.label: HDD fsync

ladder.w: A round trip (RTT) is the time for a message to reach another machine and the reply to come back. Inside one cloud region, machines sit in a few nearby data centres ("availability zones").

pts.note: Microsoft "strives to achieve" under about 2 ms between zones of a region (a target, not a measurement).
pts.label: Azure: zone to zone, target

pts.note: Azure East US to East US 2 (two nearby Virginia regions): 8 ms P50.
pts.label: East US to East US 2

ladder.w: Virginia to California and back.

pts.note: Azure East US to West US: 69 ms P50 (2026).
pts.label: East US to West US

ladder.w: Virginia to London and back. Light in glass fibre covers about 200,000 km a second, so distance sets a floor no engineering can beat.

pts.note: Floor: 2 x 5,917 km great-circle / 200,000 km/s = 59 ms. Real cables are longer than the great circle.
pts.label: physics floor

pts.note: Azure East US to UK South: 78 ms P50 (2026).
pts.label: East US to UK South

ladder.n: California to the Netherlands and back
ladder.w: Dean's classic long-haul figure, set beside today's measurement for the same route.

pts.note: Azure West US (California) to West Europe (Netherlands): 145 ms P50 (2026). Unchanged in 17 years: it is physics.
pts.label: West US to West Europe

ladder.n: Round trip to the other side of the world
ladder.w: Virginia to Sydney.

pts.note: Azure East US to Australia East: 201 ms P50.
pts.label: East US to Australia

ladder.n: Open a new HTTPS connection (TCP + TLS 1.3)
ladder.w: Before the first request, TCP needs one round trip to set up the connection and TLS 1.3 one more to agree on encryption keys (TLS 1.2 needed two). So a new connection costs two RTTs before the request even leaves.

pts.note: 2 RTT x 78 ms (Virginia to London) = 156 ms before the request is sent. TLS 1.2: 3 RTT = 234 ms. A reused connection pays 0.
pts.label: TLS 1.3, transatlantic

pts.note: 2 RTT x 8 ms (two nearby Virginia regions) = 16 ms.
pts.label: TLS 1.3, nearby region

ladder.n: Database query: indexed lookup by primary key
ladder.w: Asking PostgreSQL for one row by its key, which it finds through an index (a sorted lookup structure) instead of scanning the table. Includes the client to server hop on the same machine; in production add the network round trip.

pts.note: pgbench -S, 1 client: 0.067 ms average per query (14,846 queries/s from one connection).
pts.label: laptop, loopback

ladder.w: A small write transaction (three updates, a select, an insert) and its commit. A commit is durable only after the database flushes its write-ahead log with an fsync: the fsync rungs above decide this number.

pts.note: Default wal_sync_method (open_datasync) on macOS: 0.421 ms, but the drive cache is not flushed.
pts.label: no real flush

pts.note: wal_sync_method = fsync_writethrough (real flush): 6.327 ms, 15 times slower; 158 commits/s from one connection.
pts.label: real flush

ladder.w: An in-memory key-value store: a lookup is a hash-table probe, a few microseconds of server work. What you feel is the network round trip plus queueing.

pts.note: redis-benchmark SET, p50 0.143 ms with 50 parallel clients on loopback (Redis docs example; machine not stated).
pts.label: docs example, p50

ladder.n: A real web page render (Stack Overflow, 2016)
ladder.w: Server time for a whole page: many cache hits and a few SQL queries, glued together by application code.

pts.note: 22.71 ms average for 49,180,275 question-page renders on 2016-02-09 (19.12 ms in ASP.NET).
pts.label: question page

ladder.n: GPU reads 1 GB from its own memory (HBM)
ladder.w: High-bandwidth memory (HBM) is the GPU's RAM, stacked beside the chip. Its bandwidth sets how fast a model can generate tokens.

pts.note: 1 GB / 8 TB/s (B200: 64 TB/s across 8 GPUs) = 0.125 ms.
pts.label: B200

ladder.w: NVLink is NVIDIA's direct GPU-to-GPU link inside a server. The quoted figures add both directions.

pts.note: H100: 900 GB/s total, so 450 GB/s each way: 1 GB in 2.2 ms.
pts.label: H100 NVLink

pts.note: B200: 14.4 TB/s / 8 = 1.8 TB/s total, 900 GB/s each way: 1.1 ms.
pts.label: B200 NVLink

ladder.n: Move 1 GB CPU to GPU (PCIe Gen5 x16)
ladder.w: PCIe is the slot that connects the GPU to the rest of the server. Loading weights from host memory goes through it.

pts.note: 128 GB/s total, 64 GB/s each way: 1 GB in 15.6 ms.
pts.label: PCIe Gen5

ladder.w: Decoding: producing the next token. With one request at a time the GPU must read every weight once per token, so memory bandwidth, not arithmetic, sets the speed.

pts.note: Floor: 3.83 GB of weights / 3.35 TB/s = 1.14 ms per token.
pts.label: bandwidth floor

pts.note: Llama 2 7B Q4_0 on an H100 80 GB, llama.cpp tg128 = 267.81 tokens/s, so 3.73 ms per token: 31% of the bandwidth floor.
pts.label: measured, H100

ladder.w: Prefill: the model reads the whole prompt in one parallel pass before the first output token. This is most of the time to first token (TTFT) when nothing is queued.

pts.note: Llama 2 7B Q4_0, H100, pp512 = 9,918.34 tokens/s: 512 tokens in 51.6 ms. Add network, queueing and batching delays for a real TTFT.
pts.label: measured, H100

ladder.w: Prefill plus 300 decode steps, one request alone on the GPU (derived from the two rungs above).

pts.note: 52 ms + 300 x 3.73 ms = 1.17 s for a 7B model; larger models are proportionally slower.
pts.label: 7B, batch 1

ladder.n: LLM: load a model onto a GPU (cold start)
ladder.w: Starting a model server: copy tens of gigabytes of weights into GPU memory, compile and warm up. Web servers start in seconds; model servers in minutes.

pts.note: "Reload models on-demand: 30-100+ seconds per switch" (vLLM blog, 2025), before any new machine has to be provisioned.
pts.label: 30 to 100+ s

budget.q: Your server (Virginia) calls a model API hosted in California for each chat reply. The user is in London.

before.note: Half of the 78 ms transatlantic round trip.
Illustrative: parse, authenticate, build the prompt.

before.lab: New TCP connection to the API
before.note: TCP needs one round trip (69 ms, Virginia to California) before any data moves.
One more round trip to agree encryption keys.

before.lab: Send prompt, wait for first token
before.note: One round trip (69 ms) plus prefill of a 512-token prompt (52 ms, 7B model on an H100).

after.lab: Send prompt on an open, pooled connection
after.note: A connection pool keeps connections open between requests, so the two handshake round trips are paid once, not per request.

budget.lesson: Two of the round trips were setup, not work. Connection reuse (HTTP keep-alive, a client-side pool) removes them; the cost is managing idle connections and their limits.

budget.n: Move slow work off the request path
budget.q: Sending a chat message also generates a conversation title with a small model and records an analytics event with a third-party service in California.

before.note: 0.421 ms of transaction work (measured) plus one 0.74 ms fsync on a network disk (Hyperdisk, measured by Callaghan).

before.lab: Generate a title with a 7B model
before.note: 2 ms round trip + 52 ms prefill + 12 tokens x 3.7 ms.

after.lab: Put two jobs on a queue
after.note: Kafka p99 of 5 ms at 200 MB/s with three replicas (Confluent 2020, fsync off, Kafka's default): the job is held on three brokers, so you can reply.
A background worker takes the job from the queue after the user already has the reply.

budget.lesson: The user waits only for what the reply needs. The rest still happens, later, on a worker; the cost is a queue to run, at-least-once delivery (a job can run twice) and a title that appears a moment after the message.

budget.q: Opening the conversation list runs one query for the list, then one more per conversation for its title: 21 queries for 20 conversations, each a round trip to a database in another zone (the "N+1 queries" pattern).

before.note: 21 x (2 ms zone round trip + 0.067 ms indexed lookup). The round trips, not the queries, are the cost.

after.lab: One cache read (the whole list, precomputed)
after.note: One round trip plus a Redis GET (0.143 ms p50 under load, Redis docs).

budget.lesson: The cache turned 21 round trips into 1. What is left is the user's own 78 ms round trip across the Atlantic, which no server-side change can remove: the next step is serving from a region near the user. The cache's cost: stale data until it is invalidated, and one more system to run.

drills.ask: Twitter said it takes in "more than 500 million Tweets a day". How many per second on average, and what peak should it plan for?

check.text: Twitter: "about 5,700 Tweets a second, on average"; record one-second peak 143,199 on 2013-08-03, "around 25 times greater than our steady state".
check.by_construction: The peak factor 25 comes from the same post, so the peak matches by construction; the average matches independently.

drills.ask: Stack Overflow's load balancers saw 209,420,973 HTTP requests on 2016-02-09, and sent 1.24 TB of HTTP traffic. How many requests per second, how much bandwidth, and how many web servers?

check.text: Stack Overflow ran this on 9 primary web servers. 1.24 TB / 209.4 M requests = 5.92 KB average response; the peak factor 2 and 539 requests/s per server are assumptions chosen so that 9 servers come out.
check.by_construction: Response size and servers per peak are back-solved from the post, so those match by construction; the per-second rate is plain arithmetic.

drills.n: GPUs for a chat feature (1 M daily users)
drills.ask: A chat assistant with 1 million daily users, 10 messages each (10 million a day, the Reading's estimate), 1,000 input and 400 output tokens per reply (the Reading's and the Scale simulator's request shape), served with Llama 3.3 70B on rented H100s. How many GPUs, and what do they cost?

check.text: Compare the cost per million output tokens with what API providers charge for the same open model: $0.32 to $2.25 per million output tokens on OpenRouter.
check.by_construction: GPU throughput is NVIDIA's maximum-throughput figure per GPU (vendor, repo commit 8a9c66c); the 50% derate for interactive speed is illustrative; the peak factor 2 matches the Reading and the Scale simulator (a daily peak about twice the average, an assumption, not a measurement).

drills.ask: Store every message and reply: about 100 tokens in, 300 out, at about 4 characters per token, plus 200 bytes of metadata. How much disk a year, with 3 copies?

check.text: OpenAI: "1 token is approximately 4 characters" (English). (100 + 300) x 4 + 200 = 1,800 bytes per message.
check.by_construction: Message sizes are illustrative; the 4 characters per token is OpenAI's rule of thumb.

drills.ask: Each daily user loads 20 images of 200 KB from your servers on AWS. What is the monthly internet egress bill?

check.text: AWS us-east-1 tiers: $0.09/GB for the first 10 TB a month, $0.085 next 40 TB, $0.07 next 100 TB, $0.05 beyond (price list of 2026-09-16).
check.by_construction: Prices are AWS list prices; the traffic is illustrative. A CDN or a provider with free egress changes the answer, which is the point.
